title: Performance of Contract
outcomes: Explain the duty to perform (Section 37), actual and attempted performance, and the conditions of a valid tender.
Decide who must perform (Sections 40–42), distinguish succession from assignment, and compute the liabilities of joint promisors (Sections 43–45).
Apply the rules on time and place (Sections 46–50), reciprocal promises and impossibility (Sections 51–58) and appropriation of payments (Sections 59–61).
Explain contracts that need not be performed (Sections 62–67) and every mode of discharge of a contract.

meta.exam_tip: Numerical-style law problems come from this unit: joint promisors with an insolvent co-promisor (Section 43) and appropriation of payments (Sections 59–61). Show the arithmetic in a small table and end with a clear conclusion.

concepts.title: Performance — Section 37; actual and attempted
body: Performance means carrying out the obligations under the contract. Section 37: the parties must perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless performance is dispensed with or excused under the Contract Act or any other law.
Actual performance: the promisor does exactly what he undertook, at the time and in the manner agreed (e.g. a borrower repays on the due date). The obligation is discharged.

Attempted performance (tender): the promisor offers to perform, but the promisee refuses. Under Section 38, when a proper offer to perform is turned down, the promisor is not liable for the failure to perform, and his own rights under the contract remain intact.
Section 37 also binds the promisor's legal representatives after his death, unless the contract shows a contrary intention (e.g. it depends on personal skill).

head: Condition
Meaning / example
rows: Unconditional
Offering to repay a loan only if the lender returns an unrelated document is not a valid tender
Whole obligation
Offering 80 of 100 bags, or the principal without the interest due, is not a valid tender
Proper time and place
Delivery at midnight, or at a place other than agreed, is not valid unless so agreed
Reasonable opportunity to inspect
The promisee must be able to check the goods are as contracted (quality and quantity)
To the proper person
Made to the promisee or his authorised agent; tender to one of several joint promisees is enough
By a person able and willing
The promisor must be in a position to perform at that moment
blocks.title: A valid tender (offer to perform)

concepts.analogy: Tender is knocking on the door with the goods in hand at the agreed hour. If the buyer refuses to open, the seller has done his part.
concepts.work: Where a customer refuses delivery, a finance controller asks the logistics team for proof of a valid tender (time, place, full quantity, chance to inspect) before booking a claim against the customer.

concepts.title: By whom must a contract be performed? (Sections 40–42)
body: Promisor himself (Section 40): where the parties intended personal performance — contracts involving personal skill, taste or confidence (a portrait, a concert, a surgery) — only the promisor can perform.
Agent: where personal skill is not the basis, the promisor (or his representative) can get the work done through any capable person.

Legal representatives: on the promisor's death, contracts not depending on personal skill bind his legal representatives — but only up to the value of the estate they inherit. A personal-skill contract ends on the promisor's death.

Third person (Section 41): once the promisee has accepted performance from an outsider, he loses the right to demand it again from the promisor — the promisor stands discharged to that extent, even if he never authorised the third person.

Joint promisors (Section 42): unless the contract says otherwise, joint promisors must perform jointly during their lives; after one dies, his legal representative performs jointly with the survivors; after the last survivor dies, the representatives of all must perform.
concepts.analogy: If you hire a famous singer, you get the singer — not her cousin. If you order cement, any reliable delivery van will do.
concepts.work: On a partner's death, a CA checks which of the firm's contracts depend on that partner's personal skill (they end) and which bind his estate (they continue).

concepts.title: Succession vs assignment
body: Succession is transfer by operation of law (e.g. on death): both rights and liabilities pass to the legal heirs, but liabilities only up to the value of the property inherited. A son inheriting ₹10 lakh of assets is not liable for his father's debts beyond ₹10 lakh.

Assignment is transfer by act of the parties: only the benefit (rights) of a contract can be assigned — a creditor may assign a debt, and the assignee can recover it from the debtor. Liabilities cannot be assigned without the creditor's consent, since that would bring in a new debtor (which needs novation). Benefits coupled with liabilities, or founded on personal skill or confidence, cannot be assigned.
concepts.analogy: Succession hands over the whole bag — gifts and bills — but you never pay more bills than the gifts are worth. Assignment hands over only the gifts.
concepts.work: In receivable financing, a company assigns its book debts to a bank or factor — the right to collect is transferred; the company's own obligations to its suppliers are not.

concepts.title: Joint promisors and joint promisees (Sections 43–45)
body: Section 43: where several persons have promised jointly, the promisee (unless the contract says otherwise) can require any one or more of them to carry out the entire promise. Liability is therefore joint and several.

Contribution: each joint promisor may compel every other to contribute equally, unless the contract shows a different intention. If one of them defaults in contributing, the others bear the loss from that default in equal shares.
The rule does not stop a surety from recovering from the principal debtor what he paid, nor allow the principal to recover from the surety.
Section 44: release of one joint promisor by the promisee does not discharge the others, and does not free the released promisor from his liability to the other joint promisors (for contribution).

Section 45: when a promise is made to two or more persons jointly, the right to claim performance rests with all of them jointly during their lives; after one dies, with his representative jointly with the survivors; after the last survivor, with the representatives of all jointly.
concepts.analogy: Joint promisors are climbers on one rope: the creditor can pull on any one of them for the whole weight; they then settle among themselves.
concepts.work: When a lender recovers a joint loan from one co-borrower, the CA computes that co-borrower's contribution claims against the others, including the loss from an insolvent co-borrower.

concepts.title: Time and place for performance (Sections 46–50)
body: The rules depend on whether a time or place is fixed and whether the promisee must first apply (ask) for performance. See the table.

Example under Section 47: goods to be delivered "on 10 March" must be offered during usual business hours that day at the usual place; delivery tendered at 10 p.m. after the business has closed can be refused.

head: Section
Situation
Rule
rows: No application needed; no time fixed
Perform within a reasonable time (a question of fact)
Day fixed; no application needed
Perform on that day during usual business hours, at the proper place
Day fixed; promisee must apply
Promisee must apply at a proper place within usual business hours
No application needed; no place fixed
Promisor must ask the promisee to appoint a reasonable place and perform there
Promisee prescribes or approves a manner or time
Performance in that manner or at that time is good performance
blocks.title: Time and place of performance (Sections 46–50)

concepts.analogy: If no clock is set, the law reads "reasonable time"; if a day is set, it reads "business hours on that day".
concepts.work: Cut-off for revenue recognition and penalty clauses often turns on whether delivery was tendered at the proper time and place.

concepts.title: Reciprocal promises (Sections 51–58)
body: Reciprocal promises are promises that form the consideration for each other. They may be mutual and concurrent (performed together — payment against delivery), mutual and dependent (one must be performed first — build the house, then get paid), or mutual and independent (each performs regardless of the other).

Section 55 is very important for problems: decide first whether time was of the essence (look at the terms and the nature of the contract — e.g. seasonal goods, a fixed event). If yes, delay makes the contract voidable at the promisee's option; if no, the promisee only gets compensation. A promisee who accepts late performance must give notice then and there to keep his right to compensation.

Section 56: initial impossibility (e.g. discovering treasure by magic) makes the agreement void. Supervening impossibility — performance becoming impossible or unlawful after the contract, by an event the promisor could not prevent (destruction of subject-matter, change of law, outbreak of war, death or incapacity in a personal contract) — makes the contract void from then. A promisor who knew, or with reasonable diligence could have known, of the impossibility must compensate a promisee who did not know.

head: Section
Rule
rows: Simultaneous reciprocal promises: a promisor need not perform unless the promisee is ready and willing to perform
Perform in the order fixed by the contract; if none, in the order the nature of the transaction requires
A party who is prevented from performing by the other may choose to avoid the contract, and may claim compensation
If the party who must perform first fails, he cannot claim the other's performance and must compensate the other

Time of essence: failure makes the contract voidable at the promisee's option. Not of essence: not voidable, but compensation for loss. Accepting late performance bars compensation unless notice is given at the time of acceptance

Agreement to do an impossible act is void; a contract becomes void when performance later becomes impossible or unlawful; a promisor who knew (or should have known) of the impossibility must compensate the promisee who did not
Reciprocal promises to do legal things and also illegal things: the legal part is a valid contract, the illegal part is void
Alternative promise with one branch illegal: only the legal branch can be enforced
blocks.title: Reciprocal promises (Sections 51–58)

concepts.analogy: Reciprocal promises are a dance: who leads, who follows, and what happens if one partner never turns up.
concepts.work: Force majeure and "time is of the essence" clauses in supply contracts are tested against Sections 55 and 56 when deliveries are delayed or become impossible.

concepts.title: Appropriation of payments (Sections 59–61)
body: When a debtor owes several separate debts to the same creditor and pays an amount that does not cover all of them, the payment must be adjusted (appropriated) in this order of rules:
Section 59 — debtor's choice: if the debtor expressly says, or circumstances show, which debt the payment is for, and the creditor accepts it, it must be applied to that debt.

Section 60 — creditor's choice: if the debtor gives no indication, the creditor is free to adjust it against any lawful debt then due and payable to him — even a debt barred by limitation. He cannot apply it to a disputed or not-yet-due debt.

Section 61 — neither appropriates: the payment is applied to the debts in order of time, whether or not they are time-barred. If the debts are of equal standing, it is applied to each proportionately.
concepts.analogy: First the payer chooses the pocket; if he is silent, the receiver chooses; if both are silent, the oldest pocket is filled first.
concepts.work: Receivables ageing and interest claims depend on which invoices a payment was applied to. CAs check remittance advices (debtor's appropriation) before allocating receipts in the ledger.

concepts.title: Contracts that need not be performed (Sections 62–67)
body: Section 62 — novation, rescission, alteration: where the parties agree to replace the contract with a new one, or to cancel or change it, the old contract no longer has to be performed. Novation replaces an existing contract with a new one (between the same or different parties) — it must be agreed before the time for performance expires. Alteration changes some terms between the same parties. Rescission cancels the contract (by agreement, or by the aggrieved party after breach).

Section 63 — remission and waiver: a promisee may dispense with or remit performance wholly or partly, extend the time, or accept any satisfaction he thinks fit instead. Accepting a smaller sum in full settlement discharges the whole debt — even without fresh consideration.
Section 64: when a person entitled to avoid a voidable contract rescinds it, the other party need not perform; the rescinding party must restore any benefit he received.

Section 65: where an agreement turns out to be void, or a contract later becomes void, whoever has received a benefit under it must give it back or pay for it (e.g. an advance paid to a singer who falls ill must be refunded).
Section 66: rescission of a voidable contract is communicated or revoked in the same way, and subject to the same rules, as a proposal.
Section 67: if the promisee neglects or refuses to give the promisor reasonable facilities for performance, the promisor is excused for non-performance caused by it.
concepts.analogy: Novation is a new rule book; alteration is crossing out a few lines; rescission is tearing up the book; remission is the referee saying "that's enough, call it done".
concepts.work: Debt restructuring (new lender, new terms) is novation; extending a payment date is alteration or remission; a one-time settlement for less than the dues is remission under Section 63 — each has a different accounting effect.

concepts.title: Discharge of a contract — the modes
body: By performance — actual or attempted (valid tender).
By mutual agreement — novation, rescission, alteration, remission (Sections 62–63).
By impossibility of performance — initial or supervening (Section 56).
By lapse of time — if the promisee does not sue within the limitation period (generally three years for money claims under the Limitation Act, 1963), the remedy is lost.
By operation of law — death (in personal contracts), insolvency, merger, unauthorised material alteration of a written document.
By breach — actual or anticipatory; the injured party is discharged from his own performance and may claim damages.

Also: remission (Section 63), neglect of the promisee to afford facilities (Section 67), and merger — where an inferior right and a superior right meet in the same person (a tenant who buys the house: the lease merges into ownership).
concepts.analogy: A contract can end because it was kept, called off, made impossible, left too late, ended by law, or broken.
concepts.work: Before writing back a liability, the CA must identify the mode of discharge — paid, waived, settled, time-barred or otherwise — and keep evidence for it.

illustrations.title: Joint promisors — one insolvent
illustrations.q: A, B and C jointly promise to pay D ₹4,50,000. D compels C to pay the whole amount. A becomes insolvent and his estate pays 40 paise in the rupee. How much can C recover from A's estate and from B, and what loss does C finally bear?

solution.provision: Section 43: the promisee may compel any one of the joint promisors to perform the whole. Each joint promisor may compel the others to contribute equally; if one defaults, the remaining promisors bear the loss from that default in equal shares.
solution.facts: C paid the whole ₹4,50,000. Each one's equal share is ₹1,50,000. A's estate can pay only 40%.
solution.analysis: C recovers A's share to the extent of A's estate; the unpaid part of A's share is shared equally by B and C.
solution.conclusion: C recovers ₹60,000 from A's estate and ₹1,95,000 from B, and finally bears ₹1,95,000 himself.

illustrations.title: Appropriation — neither party appropriates
illustrations.q: Kapil owes Mehra & Co. three separate debts: debt 1 ₹30,000 due in January 2021 (now time-barred), debt 2 ₹45,000 due in March 2024, and debt 3 ₹25,000 due in August 2025. In 2026 he sends ₹60,000 without saying which debt it is for, and Mehra & Co. also makes no appropriation. How is the payment applied?

solution.provision: Section 61: where neither the debtor nor the creditor appropriates, the payment is applied to the debts in order of time, whether or not they are barred by limitation.
solution.facts: Three debts in date order: ₹30,000 (time-barred), ₹45,000, ₹25,000. Payment ₹60,000; no appropriation by either side.
solution.analysis: Apply first to the oldest debt (the time-barred debt counts), then to the next in time.
solution.conclusion: Debt 1 is fully paid (₹30,000); ₹30,000 goes to debt 2, leaving ₹15,000 of debt 2 and the whole of debt 3 (₹25,000) outstanding — ₹40,000 in all.

illustrations.title: Personal-skill contract and the death of the promisor
illustrations.q: Ms. Rao pays a well-known sculptor ₹1,50,000 in advance for a bust of her late father. The sculptor dies before starting. Ms. Rao asks the sculptor's son, also a sculptor, to complete the work; alternatively she wants her advance back. Advise.

solution.provision: Section 37 and Section 40: a contract involving personal skill or founded on personal confidence must be performed by the promisor himself and comes to an end on his death; legal representatives are not bound to perform it. Section 65: when a contract becomes void, a person who received an advantage under it must restore it.
solution.facts: The contract was for the sculptor's own artistic skill. He died before performance. He had received ₹1,50,000 in advance.
solution.analysis: The son is not bound to make the bust, and Ms. Rao cannot insist that he do so. The contract became void on the sculptor's death, so the advance must be restored out of his estate.
solution.conclusion: Ms. Rao cannot compel the son to complete the work, but she can recover the advance of ₹1,50,000 from the sculptor's legal representatives (to the extent of the estate inherited).

illustrations.title: Time of the essence — late delivery of festival stock
illustrations.q: Diya Crackers Ltd. agrees to deliver fireworks to a retailer "by 25 October, time being of the essence", for the Diwali season. It delivers on 3 November. The retailer accepts the goods without any comment and later claims compensation for lost Diwali sales. Decide.

solution.provision: Section 55: if time is of the essence and the promisor fails to perform in time, the contract becomes voidable at the promisee's option. A promisee who accepts the late performance loses his claim for compensation for the delay, unless he tells the promisor, when accepting, that he will claim it.
solution.facts: Time was expressly of the essence. Delivery was late. The retailer accepted the goods without giving any notice reserving a claim.
solution.analysis: The retailer could have rejected the late delivery and avoided the contract. By accepting without notice, it lost the right to compensation for the delay.
solution.conclusion: The retailer's claim for compensation fails.

jobs.title: Allocating a lump-sum receipt
jobs.role: Accounts executive in a distribution company
jobs.situation: A dealer with three overdue invoices sends ₹2 lakh by NEFT with no remittance advice.
steps: Ask the dealer whether he intends the payment for particular invoices (Section 59).
If he gives no indication, the company may choose — e.g. the oldest invoice, even a time-barred one (Section 60) — but not a disputed invoice.
Record the appropriation decision in writing and communicate it to the dealer.
If nobody appropriates, the law applies it in order of time (Section 61).
jobs.takeaway: The ledger allocation of a receipt is a legal choice — record who made it.
jobs.think: Why might a creditor prefer to apply the money to a time-barred invoice?
jobs.answer: Because the time-barred invoice cannot be recovered through a suit; applying the receipt there keeps the newer, enforceable invoices alive for recovery.

jobs.title: One-time settlement with a customer
jobs.situation: A customer owes ₹12 lakh and offers ₹9 lakh in full and final settlement. Management agrees.
steps: Accepting a smaller sum in satisfaction is remission under Section 63 — no fresh consideration is needed.
Once accepted, the balance ₹3 lakh is discharged; it cannot be claimed later.
Get a written settlement letter stating it is in full and final settlement.
Write off the ₹3 lakh with proper approval.
jobs.takeaway: A settlement letter is not a formality — it discharges the balance in law.

mcqs.q: Under Section 37, the parties to a contract must:
options: Perform or offer to perform their promises, unless excused by law
Perform only if the court orders
mcqs.explain: Section 37 — performance or offer to perform.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a requirement of a valid tender?
options: It may be for part of the obligation
It must be at the proper time and place
The promisee must have a reasonable chance to inspect
mcqs.explain: A tender must be for the whole obligation.

mcqs.q: A promises to paint a portrait for B and dies before painting it. The contract:
options: Comes to an end; A's heirs are not bound
Must be performed by A's heirs
Must be performed by any painter B chooses at A's heirs' cost
mcqs.explain: Personal-skill contracts end on the promisor's death.

mcqs.q: A owes B ₹2,00,000. C, without A's knowledge, pays B ₹1,20,000 on A's behalf and B accepts it. B can now claim from A:
mcqs.explain: Section 41 — accepted performance by a third person discharges the promisor to that extent.

mcqs.q: Which of the following can be assigned?
options: The right to receive a debt
The liability to repay a loan
A contract to sing at a concert
A benefit coupled with a personal liability
mcqs.explain: Only benefits can be assigned; liabilities and personal contracts cannot.

mcqs.q: X, Y and Z jointly promise to pay ₹90,000 to W. W may:
options: Compel any one of them to pay the whole ₹90,000
mcqs.explain: Section 43 — joint and several liability.

mcqs.q: P, Q and R jointly owe ₹3,00,000. The creditor releases P. Then:
options: Q and R remain liable for the whole; P remains liable to Q and R for contribution
Only P's share is reduced from the debt
P is free from every liability
mcqs.explain: Section 44.

mcqs.q: A, B and C jointly owe ₹4,50,000. C pays it all; A is insolvent and his estate pays 40 paise in the rupee. C can recover from B:
mcqs.explain: B's own share ₹1,50,000 + half of A's shortfall ₹45,000.

mcqs.q: Where no time is fixed and no application is needed, a promise must be performed:
mcqs.explain: Section 46.

mcqs.q: A buyer prevents a contractor from starting work. Under Section 53 the contract is:
options: Voidable at the contractor's option, with compensation
Valid and must still be performed
mcqs.explain: Section 53.

mcqs.q: Time is NOT of the essence and the promisor is late. The promisee:
options: Cannot avoid the contract but can claim compensation for loss
mcqs.explain: Section 55.

mcqs.q: A contract to sell a specific horse becomes void when the horse dies before delivery, without fault. This is:
mcqs.explain: Destruction of the subject-matter.

mcqs.q: If the debtor does not indicate which debt a payment is for, the creditor may apply it to:
options: Any lawful debt due, even a time-barred one
mcqs.explain: Section 60.

mcqs.q: Debts of ₹30,000 (oldest, time-barred), ₹45,000 and ₹25,000; ₹60,000 paid, no appropriation by either. The outstanding balance of the second debt is:
mcqs.explain: Section 61 — order of time; the oldest (even time-barred) is cleared first.

mcqs.q: Substitution of a new contract for an existing one is:
mcqs.explain: Section 62.

mcqs.q: A creditor accepts a smaller sum in full satisfaction of a larger debt. The debt is:
options: Discharged only to the amount paid
mcqs.explain: Remission needs no consideration.

mcqs.q: A tenant buys the house he occupies. His lease ends by:
mcqs.explain: The lesser right merges in ownership.

mcqs.q: Rescission of a voidable contract is communicated or revoked:
options: In the same manner as a proposal — Section 66
mcqs.explain: Section 66.

questions.q: X, Y and Z jointly borrowed ₹3,60,000 from Bank P. On the due date Bank P recovered the entire amount from Y. Z has since been declared insolvent and his estate pays 25 paise in the rupee. Explain, with reference to the Indian Contract Act, 1872, how much Y can recover from X and from Z's estate, and the loss Y finally bears.

model.provision: Section 43: where persons have made a joint promise, the promisee can require any one or more of them to carry out the entire promise. Each joint promisor may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally; if any one defaults in contributing, the remaining joint promisors bear the loss arising from the default in equal shares.
model.facts: Bank P recovered the full ₹3,60,000 from Y. Each borrower's equal share is ₹1,20,000. Z's estate pays only 25%.
model.analysis: Y can claim from Z's estate 25% of ₹1,20,000 = ₹30,000. The shortfall of ₹90,000 in Z's contribution is shared equally by X and Y. So Y recovers from X: X's own share ₹1,20,000 + half the shortfall ₹45,000 = ₹1,65,000.
model.conclusion: Y recovers ₹1,65,000 from X and ₹30,000 from Z's estate, and finally bears ₹1,65,000 himself. (Check: ₹1,65,000 + ₹1,65,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹3,60,000.)

scheme.pt: Section 43 — promisee may compel any one
Equal contribution and sharing of default
Equal share and recovery from insolvent estate
Recovery from X including half the shortfall

checks.label: equal share of X, Y and Z
Y recovers from Z's insolvent estate (25%)
Z's shortfall
Y recovers from X: own share + half the shortfall
Y finally bears
proof: X + Y + Z's estate = debt

remarks: Most errors are in sharing the shortfall — it is borne equally by the solvent promisors, not by the one who paid alone.
mistakes: Ignoring the 25% received from the insolvent estate.
Making Y bear the entire shortfall.
tips: Show a mini-table of shares in the analysis.
Add a one-line arithmetic proof that totals equal the debt.

questions.q: Mr. Vora owes Mr. Kale three debts: ₹18,000 due in June 2021 (time-barred), ₹32,000 due in May 2024 and ₹20,000 due in January 2026. He sends (i) a cheque of ₹24,000 stating it is "towards the May 2024 bill", and later (ii) a cheque of ₹40,000 without any instruction; Mr. Kale makes no appropriation. Explain how the payments will be applied.

model.text: Section 59: where the debtor indicates the debt to which a payment is to be applied, and the creditor accepts it, it must be so applied. Section 61: where neither party appropriates, the payment is applied to the debts in order of time, whether or not time-barred.

head: Step
Debt 1 — Jun 2021 (₹)
Debt 2 — May 2024 (₹)
Debt 3 — Jan 2026 (₹)
rows: Opening
Cheque (i) ₹24,000 — debtor's appropriation (S. 59)
Cheque (ii) ₹40,000 — order of time (S. 61): debt 1 cleared, then debt 2

model.text: Result: debts 1 and 2 are fully discharged; ₹6,000 of debt 3 remains outstanding. (Cheque (ii): ₹40,000 − ₹18,000 = ₹22,000; ₹22,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹14,000 applied to debt 3.)

then the balance of debt 2 is cleared

remarks: Candidates must respect the debtor's instruction for the first cheque before applying the order-of-time rule to the second.
mistakes: Applying cheque (i) to the oldest debt despite the debtor's instruction.
Skipping the time-barred debt under Section 61.
tips: A running table of balances makes the answer easy to mark.

model.text: Both require mutual consent and are covered by Section 62; novation must take place before the time for performance expires.

remarks: The point that novation may involve new parties earns a separate mark.
mistakes: Saying alteration can bring in a new party.

questions.q: State the various modes by which a contract may be discharged.

items: By performance — actual, or attempted through a valid tender (Sections 37, 38).
By mutual agreement — novation, rescission, alteration (Section 62) and remission (Section 63).
By lapse of time — expiry of the limitation period under the Limitation Act, 1963.
By operation of law — death in personal contracts, insolvency, unauthorised material alteration.
By the promisee's neglect to afford reasonable facilities (Section 67).
By merger of an inferior right into a superior right.

scheme.pt: Lapse of time and operation of law

remarks: A brief line with an example under each mode is ideal.
tips: Number the modes; give section numbers where they exist.

summary: Section 37: perform or offer to perform. Valid tender: unconditional, whole, proper time and place, chance to inspect, proper person (Section 38).
Who performs: promisor (personal skill), agent, legal representatives (up to estate), third person accepted by promisee (Section 41), joint promisors jointly (Section 42).
Succession passes rights and liabilities (liability limited to estate); assignment passes only benefits.
Section 43: promisee may sue any joint promisor for the whole; equal contribution; default shared equally. Section 44: release of one does not discharge others. Section 45: joint promisees.
Sections 46–50 time and place; 51–54 order of reciprocal promises; 55 time of essence; 56 impossibility; 57–58 legal and illegal parts.
Appropriation: debtor (59) → creditor, even time-barred (60) → order of time / proportionate (61).

Sections 62–67: novation, rescission, alteration, remission, restoration of benefits (64, 65), communication of rescission (66), promisee's neglect (67). Discharge: performance, agreement, impossibility, lapse of time, operation of law, breach.

viva.q: What are the conditions of a valid tender of performance?
viva.model: A valid tender must be unconditional, must be for the whole obligation, must be made at the proper time and place, and must give the promisee a reasonable opportunity to inspect the goods. It must be made to the proper person by a person able and willing to perform.

viva.model: The promisee may compel any one of the joint promisors, or more than one, to perform the whole promise. The one who pays can compel the others to contribute equally. If one of them defaults in contributing, the remaining joint promisors share that loss equally.

viva.q: Explain the rules for appropriation of payments.
viva.model: First, if the debtor indicates which debt the payment is for, it must be applied to that debt, under Section 59. If the debtor does not indicate, the creditor may apply it to any lawful debt due, even a time-barred debt, under Section 60. If neither of them appropriates, it is applied in order of time under Section 61, and proportionately if the debts are of equal standing.

viva.model: A contract may be discharged by performance, by mutual agreement such as novation, rescission or alteration, by impossibility of performance, by lapse of time, by operation of law such as death or insolvency, and by breach of contract.

viva.q: What happens when performance becomes impossible after the contract is made?
viva.model: Under Section 56, when performance becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made, because of an event the promisor could not prevent, the contract becomes void. Examples are destruction of the subject-matter, change of law, war, or death or illness in a personal contract. If the promisor knew of the impossibility and the promisee did not, the promisor must compensate the promisee.

viva.q: What is the effect of failure to perform at the fixed time under Section 55?
viva.model: If time is of the essence, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the promisee. If time is not of the essence, the contract is not voidable, but the promisee can claim compensation for the loss. If the promisee accepts late performance, he cannot claim compensation unless he gives notice at the time of acceptance.

cases.title: Shah Brothers settle their accounts
cases.case: Shah Brothers, a wholesaler, is owed three separate amounts by Pinto Stores: ₹50,000 due in 2021 (now time-barred), ₹70,000 due in 2024 and ₹30,000 due in 2025. Pinto sends ₹1,00,000 with no instructions, and Shah Brothers does not appropriate it either. Shah Brothers also had a contract to supply Pinto 500 crates of mangoes "by 15 May, time being of the essence"; it delivered on 25 May and Pinto accepted, writing on the delivery note: "Accepted late — we reserve our claim for loss." Separately, three partners of Pinto had jointly borrowed ₹3,00,000 from Shah Brothers, which has now released one of them.

mcqs.q: How much of the ₹1,00,000 goes to the 2021 debt?
mcqs.explain: Section 61 — order of time, including time-barred debts: the 2021 debt of ₹50,000 is cleared first.

mcqs.q: What total remains due from Pinto after the payment?
Can Pinto claim compensation for the late mango delivery?
options: Yes — it gave notice at the time of accepting late performance
No — accepting late performance always bars compensation
No — time was of the essence, so only rescission was possible
mcqs.explain: Section 55 — notice at acceptance preserves the claim.

mcqs.q: After Shah Brothers releases one of the three borrowing partners:
options: The other two remain liable for the whole ₹3,00,000
The debt is reduced by ₹1,00,000 automatically
The released partner must still pay Shah Brothers
mcqs.explain: Section 44 — release of one joint promisor does not discharge the others (and he remains liable to them for contribution).
